client: Honestly, ever since I got diagnosed with this chronic condition, I just can't stop thinking about how my life is basically over. Every morning I wake up and immediately think about all the things I won't be able to do anymore, and it makes me so scared and angry. I don't even know if talking about it will help - it's not like words can change the facts.
therapist: I hear how deeply this diagnosis has shaken you, and how those automatic thoughts about lost possibilities feel so overwhelming each morning. Your feelings of fear and anger make complete sense given this major life change. What would it be like to explore both the losses you're facing and the possibilities that might still remain?

client: I guess I could try to think about what's still possible, but it's hard when everything feels so limited now. Part of me worries that if I focus on the positives, I'm just fooling myself or pretending things aren't as bad as they really are. It's like, how do I balance accepting the reality with finding hope?
therapist: That's such an important tension you're noticing - between acknowledging the real challenges while also looking for meaningful ways forward. Perhaps we could explore what "acceptance" means to you, because it doesn't have to mean giving up hope or pretending the difficulties don't exist. What might a balanced middle ground look like for you in this situation?

client: I don't know, when I think about acceptance it just feels like surrendering to this terrible thing. But I guess a middle ground would be... maybe acknowledging that some things have changed while still finding value in what I can do? It's just hard because grieving what I've lost takes up so much space right now.
therapist: You're doing important work by recognizing both your grief and your curiosity about how to move forward. The grieving process naturally takes up space, and it's okay that this feels overwhelming right now. What small, meaningful activities might help you begin to reconnect with parts of yourself that aren't defined by your condition?

client: I used to love sketching, but lately I haven't even touched my sketchbook because I think "what's the point if I can't do all the art projects I dreamed of?" But maybe I could try just doodling again... though part of me feels like that's such a small thing compared to what I've lost. It's frustrating.
therapist: I hear both the frustration about your changed dreams and that tentative spark of interest in sketching again - that small step matters more than it might seem right now. When we're grieving big losses, sometimes reconnecting with familiar joys in new ways can help us rediscover meaning. What might it feel like to approach sketching just as an experiment, without putting pressure on it to replace what's been lost?

client: I guess I could try sketching as an experiment, but I'm worried I'll just get frustrated if it doesn't feel the same as before. Part of me thinks maybe I should wait until I feel more ready, because trying something I used to love and having it feel different might just make me feel worse. It's scary to think about how things might have changed.
therapist: Your hesitation makes complete sense - it's natural to feel protective of something that brought you joy and to worry about how it might feel different now. What if we framed this as an opportunity to explore what sketching means to you in this new chapter of your life, rather than comparing it to before?

client: I guess reframing it as a new chapter could help, but it still feels like I'm losing something precious. What if I try sketching and find that I can't enjoy it anymore? That thought terrifies me because it was such a big part of who I was. Maybe I'm not ready to find out yet.
therapist: Your deep connection to sketching and fear of losing that part of yourself shows how meaningful it has been in your life. It's okay to take time with this - there's no rush to confront these changes before you feel ready. What might help you feel more prepared to explore this when the time feels right?

client: Maybe if I started with just looking through my old sketchbooks first, instead of jumping into drawing. That way I could remember the joy without the pressure to perform. But I'm still scared that even looking at them will make me sad about what I've lost. It feels like no matter what I do, the grief is right there waiting.
therapist: That sounds like a gentle first step - reconnecting with the memories before diving back into creating. The grief will likely be there, but perhaps alongside it might be moments of appreciation for what your art has meant to you. What would it be like to approach looking through your sketchbooks as an experiment in noticing both the sadness and any other feelings that might arise?

client: I could try that, but I'm worried I'll just fixate on all the drawings I did when I was healthier and feel worse. Maybe I should pick just one sketchbook instead of all of them - but then part of me thinks that's avoiding the real pain. It's so confusing trying to figure out how much to feel versus how much to protect myself.
therapist: You're showing such self-awareness in recognizing both your need to protect yourself and your desire to fully process these feelings - that balance is difficult for anyone facing profound changes. Perhaps we could explore what "enough" feeling looks like for you - not complete avoidance nor complete immersion, but somewhere that honors both your pain and your need for self-care. What small experiment with the sketchbooks might feel manageable while still meaningful?

client: Maybe I could set a timer for just 10 minutes with one sketchbook, and promise myself I'll stop after that no matter what. That way it wouldn't feel so overwhelming. But I'm still scared that even that small amount will open floodgates I can't close - I don't trust myself to stay regulated when I think about what I've lost.
therapist: That sounds like a thoughtful, measured approach - setting both a time limit and clear boundaries for yourself shows real self-compassion. Your concern about the floodgates opening is understandable; would it help to plan some grounding techniques for after the 10 minutes, like a comforting activity or calling a supportive friend?

client: Having a plan for afterwards might help, but honestly most of my friends don't really understand what I'm going through. I think I'd just feel worse if I called someone and they gave me some generic "stay positive" advice. Maybe I could make some tea afterwards instead - that's something I can do alone that usually calms me down a little.
therapist: I love how you're identifying what truly comforts you - tea sounds like a perfect, gentle way to transition after looking at your sketches. It's okay that not everyone understands what you're experiencing right now; trusting your own instincts about what helps is so important. What might it feel like to approach this whole experiment - the sketching time, the tea afterwards - with curiosity rather than expectations about how it "should" go?
